data_and_models: Clinic profiles, patient interaction logs and KPI snapshots in MongoDB; patient history is passed into a structured Gemini prompt to write each reactivation message, so identifiable clinical and appointment history leaves the product on every agent turn. Inbound sources are the clinic's own systems through the audit questionnaire plus Google Calendar, Google My Business and Twilio/Gmail; the message channels are SMS and email. No model is trained or fine-tuned. Nothing on the page addresses HIPAA, a business associate agreement with the model or messaging providers, patient consent to be messaged by an automated system, de-identification before the prompt, encryption at rest, or who can read the interaction logs - and the stated expansion is into medical clinics, optometry and physiotherapy, i.e. the same patient-data surface with more of it.
limits_admitted: no direct practice-management integration at launch: Dentrix, Eaglesoft and Excel are absorbed by the audit questionnaire instead, which is why native connectors are the next item
message tone needed prompt engineering and a staff rating loop before the output sounded like the clinic rather than a chatbot
full autonomy was deliberately withheld: for the first two weeks every message is reviewed before sending
the first dashboard was too wide to use and was cut from around 40 metrics to 12
name: DentOps

numbers.arithmetic: does not reconcile with the page's own production log: '84 agent actions executed in production (logged and verifiable)'. A recovery is at minimum one outbound message, one reply handled and one booking, so 330 recoveries at one clinic is hundreds of logged actions before any of the other two agents are counted. It also fails against their own unit value: the audit pitch prices lapsed patients at about $14,000 for 47 of them, i.e. $298 each, so 330 recovered in a month is roughly $98,000 of recalled revenue per clinic - which does not sit inside the two-chair practice the whole page is written for, and would make a $249 per month subscription absurdly underpriced
numbers.claim: 330 lapsed patients recovered per clinic on average in the first 30 days

numbers.arithmetic: not falsifiable from the page: the number of clinics in 'active' is never given, the measurement window before and after is not defined, and the 18% figure is also used as the example clinic's baseline inside the KPI copy, so the same number is doing two jobs - a halving may be real and is unlocatable either way
numbers.claim: no-show rate fell from 18% to 9% across active clinics

numbers.arithmetic: structural, and the sharpest number on the page: small enough to be a real production log rather than a demo, described as verifiable, and it is what contradicts the 330-patient claim. 84 actions across even two clinics is a trickle, which is what 15 clinics 'demoed' rather than 'live' would predict
numbers.denominator: the activity feed's log, over an unstated number of clinics and days

one_line: An AI operations layer for a two-chair dental practice: a 20-minute audit prices the leaks, a small agent team sends recall and no-show messages behind a two-week approval gate, and twelve KPIs on one dashboard explain themselves in plain English.

sections.accomplishments: Idea to interested customers in under five weeks, fifteen dental clinics demoed at $249 per month, and the whole platform - audit engine, agent orchestration, live dashboard - built by two people on the Google AI stack. The performance claims are three: the Recall Agent recovered an average of 330 lapsed patients per clinic in the first 30 days; the no-show rate fell from 18% to 9% across active clinics; and 84 agent actions were executed in production, described as logged and verifiable. The sales anecdote is the same shape as the KPI design: walking a clinic through its own audit - 'you have 47 lapsed patients worth approximately $14,000 in potential revenue' - converted to paid in one call every time. No award is claimed on the page.
sections.challenges: Four difficulties, three of them about the data and one about trust. Dental data is messy - Dentrix, Eaglesoft, plain Excel - and building an intake flexible enough to normalise it without deep integrations was harder than expected, answered by the structured audit questionnaire that extracts what is needed from any source system. Agent reliability and tone: patient-facing messages had to sound clinic-branded rather than chatbot-generic, which took significant prompt engineering plus a feedback loop where clinic staff rated and adjusted message quality early. Meaningful KPIs versus vanity metrics: the first dashboard tracked around 40 measures, dentists had no time to interpret them, so it was stripped to twelve with a sentence of interpretation under each ('your no-show rate is 18%. industry average is 10%. fixing this could recover approximately $X per month'). And the biggest obstacle was not the product but permission - convincing owners to let agents message their patients - solved with the approval-first mode for the first two weeks.
sections.how_we_built_it: React, Vite and TypeScript for the dashboard, onboarding flow and agent activity feed; Node.js and Express for the REST API, agent orchestration and webhook handling; MongoDB for clinic profiles, patient interaction logs and KPI snapshots. Gemini via the Google AI Studio API powers the audit analysis, the agent reasoning, message generation and KPI interpretation. Twilio for SMS, the Gmail API for email campaigns, the Google Calendar and My Business APIs for the booking and inquiry loops. Backend in a container on Cloud Run, frontend on Firebase Hosting - a MERN stack with Google's AI layer on top, built by a two-person team. Each agent is a reasoning loop over a query: the Recall Agent pulls patients inactive 180+ days from MongoDB, passes the patient history to Gemini with a structured prompt, generates the message, sends it via Twilio and logs the interaction; a reply is handled by the same loop and booked through Google Calendar.
sections.inspiration: Dentists spend years on the craft and then spend 10-15 hours a week on operations nobody trained them for: chasing no-shows, following up with lapsed patients, answering Google inquiries, working out why the chairs are empty. The team's origin is customer contact, not a model demo - they talked to clinic owners in their network and heard the same sentence repeatedly, 'I didn't go to school for six years to send reminder texts'. The diagnosis is a market shape rather than an effort problem: the tooling available to a small clinic is either too expensive, too complex, or built for enterprise hospital systems, and the stated belief is that every clinic should be able to reach the operations intelligence that only large healthcare chains can currently afford - agents recalling lapsed patients, eliminating no-shows and following up on inquiries so the dentist works on patients instead of admin.
sections.learned: Four lessons, all about scope and trust rather than the model. Niche early and niche hard: targeting dental clinics specifically, instead of small businesses generally, made the messaging, the KPIs, the sales conversations and the agent logic all easier - 'a platform for everyone is a platform for no one'. The audit was meant to be a funnel step and turned out to be the thing clinics talked about and shared with their office manager and business partner, so it carries referral potential they had not anticipated - 'the audit is the product'. AI-native does not mean AI-everywhere: reviewing a patient's history before a message goes out is better with a human in the loop at least early, the right shape being AI doing the heavy lifting with human confirmation instead of full autonomy on day one, because trust is earned incrementally. And revenue conversations move faster when the prospect is looking at their own data.
sections.what_it_does: Onboarding is a 20-minute structured audit of the clinic's operations with existing tools connected - Google Calendar, the practice management system, or a spreadsheet if there is nothing better. Gemini analyses the answers and returns a prioritised ops gap report that says where revenue is leaking and estimates the dollar impact of each gap, rendered as a visual priority matrix. From that report the clinic gets a tailored agent team: a Recall Agent that finds patients inactive for 180+ days and sends personalised reactivation messages over SMS and email, tracking reappointment rate weekly; a No-Show Agent that runs confirmation sequences at 48 hours and 2 hours out and backfills cancelled slots from the waitlist; a New Patient Agent that answers Google My Business inquiries, follows up missed calls and requests reviews after the appointment. The dashboard carries twelve KPIs in three departments - patient ops (recall, no-show, reappointment, chair utilisation), revenue (per visit, treatment acceptance, average invoice, monthly trend) and marketing (acquisition by source, cost per new patient, review count and rating) - updated daily, with plain-English interpretation under each number. Every agent action is logged to an activity feed, and in the first two weeks nothing goes out unreviewed: the clinic approves each message before it is sent.
sections.what_next: More agents on the same loop - treatment plan follow-up for patients who were given a recommendation and never booked, insurance verification, post-treatment care messaging. Native Dentrix and Eaglesoft connectors so the onboarding audit stops needing manual data entry. Multi-location support for chains and Dental Service Organisations running 3-10 clinics on one dashboard. Then the same operations model on adjacent niches that share recurring appointments and no-show economics: medical clinics, optometry practices, physiotherapy centres. And a pre-seed raise, positioned as 'multiple clinics and growing MRR', to accelerate sales and build the integration layer.

testing: No test suite, evaluation set, harness or run link is published anywhere on the page. The quality work is described only as prompt engineering plus a staff feedback loop in which clinic users rated and adjusted message quality during early use. The one figure offered as evidence of operation is '84 agent actions executed in production (logged and verifiable)', which is a count of actions taken rather than of outcomes measured, and it is the number that contradicts the growth claim in the same section. There is no repository to look for tests in.
